newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin vows to restore order in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin vows to restore order in Russia.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, looking fiercely determined, vowed in his annual state of the nation speech on Thursday to restore order in Russia and announced he would reshuffle his government.

"Enough is enough...The time has come to restore order and I will do that," Yeltsin, 66, said in a clear and confident voice in a 25-minute speech which received a polite standing ovation from members of parliament gathered in the Kremlin.
"The structure and composition of the government must be changed. Energetic and competent people will come...and I will announce these changes in the coming days."
Yeltsin said he would launch a crusade against corruption at even the highest levels and ruled out constitutional changes to satisfy his opponents's demands for his powers to be weakened.

The overall aim of the speech was to show he is firmly back in charge after spending most of the last eight months -- and almost the entirety of his second presidential term so far -- out of the Kremlin with health problems.
He looked well and stood firmly on his feet.
"Russia has entered the year of 1997 with a heavy burden of problems. The situation in the country is extremely difficult," he said.
The prime concern, he said, was the economy.
"The rise of prices has slowed down but we did not manage to stop the fall in (industrial) output and increase the flood of investments," Yeltsin said.
Announcing the new fight against crime, he declared investigations must go up to the highest levels.
"I will resolutely punish those who break the constitution and laws. There is corruption at every level of power....there must be no untouchables," he said.
He did not announce details of his plans for a government shake-up but it was widely expected to be announced later in the day, when the government meets.

Kremlin sources said Yeltsin's chief of staff, the liberal Anatoly Chubais, could be taken on as Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's first deputy premier to spearhead the crackdown on economic crime and push through reforms.
Yeltsin chided Chernomyrdin last week for the government's poor performance and urged him to put things right immediately.
The liberal Izvestia newspaper said on Thursday that it expected Chubais to be appointed number two in the government and take charge of running everyday affairs.

It said Finance Minister Alexander Livshits, first deputy prime ministers Vladimir Potanin and Viktor Ilyushin, Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Lobov and Labour and Social Development Minister Gennady Melikyan were likely to be dismissed.
Yeltsin ruled out the constitutional amendments demanded by the opposition communists to try to water down his vast presidential powers or remove him on health grounds.
"I am against such a hurry. First we have to learn to respect the constitution...and only after that think about changes," he said.
Yeltsin attacked NATO's plans to expand eastwards, calling them an attempt to "squeeze" Russia out of Europe and said the continent would pay a heavy price for them.

"We are against NATO's plans for eastward expansion. Their realisation will deliver a direct blow to our security. Behind them is the aspiration to squeeze Russia out of Europe and to leave it politically isolated," Yeltsin said.
The speech was a summary of a longer written address handed out to members of parliament.
The text, in contrast to last year's, was short on concrete economic proposals. Some analysts suggest Yeltsin wants to give Chubais, 41, a free hand to deal with the economy.
